1.sense: The surah opens on an action with no named actor. Someone frowned and turned his face aside. The verb is third person, which holds the reproach at a small distance from the man being reproached, and the reader does not yet know who either party is.

notes.t: The third person is doing work here. Allah could have said you frowned, and two verses later He does switch to you. Starting at a distance and then closing it is the shape of the whole opening passage.

The exegetes are near unanimous that the one who frowned is the Prophet ﷺ himself, and the transmitted reports say so plainly. A minority of later writers proposed that the frowning man was some other person sitting with him. The majority position is the older one and rests on what was passed down.
notes.src: reported from Aisha by at-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim and others; the minority reading is late and has no transmitted support

notes.t: A frown is not an offence in any law book. The surah spends its first ten verses on an expression that crossed a face, which sets the standard the rest of it will apply.

links.why: the same man is told he stands on a great character
and do not repel the one who asks

2.sense: Now the cause. A blind man came to him, and that is all the verse reports. It does not say he interrupted, or raised his voice, or arrived at a bad hour, though the reports say he did interrupt. It states his arrival and his blindness and stops.

notes.t: The blind man is identified in the reports as Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, a Meccan Muslim who later called the adhan in Medina and was left in charge of the city while the Prophet ﷺ was away.
notes.src: the identification comes from the report of Aisha and is accepted by the exegetes; the details of his later service are in the biographical literature

notes.t: He is named here by what he could not do rather than by his name. Since he could not see the frown, the reproach is not for wounding him in a way he noticed. It is for the frown itself.
The Qur'an lifts certain obligations from the blind by name elsewhere, so blindness in the Book is a recognised condition of a body and not a figure of speech here.

links.why: there is no blame upon the blind, stated as law
the same exemption repeated for war

3.sense: The address turns to the second person. What would let you know. The question is less a scolding than a statement about the limits of what any person standing in a room can see. The man who looks least promising may be the one about to grow.

notes.t: Yazzakka is from the root of zakah, which carries cleansing and increase at once. The picture underneath is of a plant pruned so that it grows, not merely of something washed.
The verb is left without an object. He does not say purified of what, or purified to what degree, which keeps the whole of the man's possible future inside one word.
The construction and what would make you know is put to the Prophet ﷺ elsewhere in the Qur'an, and each time it concerns something no human being can measure, such as the nearness of the Hour.

links.why: the same construction used of the timing of the Hour
do not claim purity for yourselves, He knows who fears Him

words.g: so that it would benefit him

4.sense: A second possibility, smaller than the first. He might not be purified outright, but he might remember something, and the remembering might do him good. Both outcomes are left uncertain, and the chance of either was enough to outweigh the meeting that was going on.

notes.t: Dhikra is a reminder, not new information. The Qur'an's standing claim about itself is that it tells people something they already half know and have set down somewhere.
The benefit is made conditional twice over: perhaps he takes heed, and then perhaps the reminder benefits him. Two layers of maybe were still worth more than the certainty of a chief's attention.
The surah will call itself a reminder outright seven verses later, using the same root, which ties the reproach to the revelation it introduces.

links.why: so remind, if the reminder benefits
and remind, for the reminder benefits the believers

5.sense: The other party in the room is described, and not as rich, not as a chief, not even as a disbeliever. He is described by an attitude he holds about himself: he reckoned he needed nothing.

notes.t: Istaghna is the tenth form of the root for wealth and sufficiency, and the tenth form usually means to seek a thing or to consider oneself to have it. The word reports a self-assessment, not a bank balance.
The same verb names the cause of transgression in another early surah: man oversteps because he sees himself as needing nobody.

The commentaries name the men at that gathering, and their lists do not agree with each other. Utba and Shayba the sons of Rabia, Abu Jahl and Umayya ibn Khalaf appear in most versions, and the surah names none of them.
notes.src: the tafsir literature preserves several differing lists of those present

links.why: man oversteps when he sees himself as needing nothing
as for the one who was miserly and thought himself free of need

6.sense: To that man you turn and attend. The pronoun you is set in front of the verb, which in Arabic shifts the weight onto the person doing it rather than onto the doing.

notes.t: Tasadda is to face a thing and move towards it, the way a person turns his whole body to someone he wants to reach. It is the exact reverse of the turning away in verse one.

Nothing in the wording accuses the Prophet ﷺ of flattery or of wanting the chief's favour. He wanted the man to accept, and the wanting was for the man's sake. The verse corrects the arithmetic anyway.
The Qur'an gives him the same instruction in another surah, to keep himself with those who call on their Lord morning and evening and not let his eyes pass over them for the adornment of this life.

links.why: keep yourself with those who call on their Lord, and do not look past them
do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening

7.sense: If that man never grows, it is not on your account. The verse takes away a weight the Prophet ﷺ was carrying, which is the idea that the outcome inside another person's chest was somehow his to secure.

notes.t: The verb yazzakka, used hopefully of the blind man four verses earlier, is used here of the self-sufficient man. One purification was possible and went unattended; the other was being pursued and was never owed.

The Qur'an repeats to the Prophet ﷺ that he is the deliverer of a message and not the guarantor of its acceptance, and it says so in the plainest terms: you are only a reminder, you are not over them a controller.
What is on you and what is not on you is the division this whole passage turns on. The frown was on him. The chief's refusal was not.

links.why: you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills
would you compel people until they become believers

8.sense: The blind man is described a second time, and now by what he did rather than by what he lacked. He came, and he came at speed. A man who cannot see does not hurry across a Meccan street for something he holds casually.

notes.t: Saʿy is effort made with the body. The same root names the walking between Safa and Marwa in the Hajj, and its ordinary sense in the language is movement with a purpose behind it.
In verse two he was the blind man, defined by an absence. Here he is the one who came to you, defined by an act. The surah raises his description as it goes, without ever giving his name.
The Qur'an uses the same verb of the man who came running from the far end of the city to warn his people, which is its picture of someone who understands what is at stake.

links.why: a man came hurrying from the farthest part of the city
the day a man remembers what he strove for

9.sense: Two words, and they carry the reason the whole reproach was issued. He was afraid. Not of the men in the room, and the verse does not say of what, which leaves it as the fear that sends a person towards Allah rather than away from Him.

notes.t: Khashya in Qur'anic usage is fear that comes with knowledge of who is being feared. It is not fright, and the Qur'an says outright that it is the people who know who have it.

The two men in this passage are set against each other by exactly one thing. One considered himself free of need, the other was afraid. Rank, wealth and eyesight are left out of the comparison entirely.
The clause is a circumstantial one in Arabic, describing the state he was in while he was walking. The fear was not the reason he gave for coming; it was the condition he came in.

links.why: it is those with knowledge among His servants who fear Allah
the one who feared standing before his Lord and restrained himself

10.sense: From him you were diverted. This closes the ten opening verses and completes the pattern: two men, two attitudes, two responses, and the response landed on the wrong one.

notes.t: Talahha comes from lahw, the Qur'an's word for amusement and for whatever pulls attention off what matters. Using it of a conversation about faith with the chiefs of Quraysh is severe.

The two clauses are built to match. As for the one who considered himself free of need, you attend to him; as for the one who came to you hurrying, you are diverted from him. The symmetry makes the point without a word of comment added.
The same root names what pulled a congregation away from the Prophet ﷺ while he was standing and delivering the sermon.

links.why: they dispersed towards trade and amusement and left you standing
do not let your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah

11.sense: A hard stop, and then a change of subject. The reproach ends at this word. What follows is about the Qur'an itself, and the first thing said of it is that it is a reminder, which is what verse four said the blind man might have benefited from.

notes.t: Kalla has no smooth English equivalent. It halts what came before rather than answering it, and it appears only in the surahs of the Book's second half. The grammarians divide over whether every instance is a rejection or whether some are simple emphasis.
The pronoun it is feminine, and the nearest feminine antecedent in the surah is the reminder of verse four. A single pronoun stitches the reproach to the revelation.
Reminder is one of the Qur'an's most frequent names for itself, and it is used of the whole Book rather than of any part.

links.why: these two verses appear there word for word
and this is a blessed reminder We have sent down

12.sense: The taking of it is left with the person. Nobody is dragged to a reminder. This also closes the argument the frown opened, because if remembering is chosen, then no man's rank tells you in advance whether he will choose it.

notes.t: The sentence is short enough to work as a rule. Two words carry the condition and one carries the outcome, and there is no clause about who deserves to be told.
This verse and the one before it appear in Surat al-Muddaththir in the same order and almost the same words, which is one of the clearest verbal overlaps between two early Meccan surahs.
Whoever wills does not mean the will runs unaided. The Qur'an pairs the phrase elsewhere with the reminder that you do not will unless Allah wills, and keeps both halves.

links.why: whoever wills may take a way to his Lord, and you will only as Allah wills
so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve

13.sense: The reminder is given a location. It is in written pages, and the pages are described before anything is said about their contents. Two verses will stack adjectives on the pages and two more on the hands that hold them, and only then does the surah return to human beings.

notes.t: Suhuf is the plural of sahifa, a sheet or a page. The Qur'an uses the word for the scriptures given to Ibrahim and Musa, and for the records of deeds that are spread open on the Last Day.

Whether these pages are the preserved tablet, the sheets held by the angels, or the copies written down by the Prophet ﷺ's ﷺ scribes has been answered all three ways by serious exegetes, and the wording does not force a choice.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record the three positions without settling on one

notes.t: This is a description of a book addressed to a society that mostly did not read. Its standing is placed in where it is kept and who handles it rather than in its length or its style.

links.why: the pages of Ibrahim and Musa, named the same way
a glorious Qur'an in a preserved tablet

14.sense: Two more descriptions of the same pages: lifted up, and kept clean. Both are passive participles. Someone raised them and someone purified them, and the verse does not say who, which keeps attention on the state they are in.

notes.t: Marfuʿa can mean physically elevated, kept out of reach, or high in rank. Arabic does not force the choice between these and the exegetes did not force it either.

Mutahhara comes from tahara, the root of ritual purity, the same root as the wudu a person makes before handling a copy of the Qur'an. The pages are described as clean before any human hand is mentioned.
The Qur'an uses the same participle of the pages a messenger recites, in a surah that describes what the People of the Book were waiting for.

links.why: a noble Qur'an in a hidden book, touched only by the purified
a messenger reciting purified pages

15.sense: The pages are held by somebody. Whoever the safara are, they are described by an occupation rather than by a rank, and the occupation is the handling of writing.

notes.t: Safara is read as the angels who carry the revelation and as scribes in general. The root gives sifr, a book, and safir, an envoy who goes between two parties. Most exegetes take them here as angels.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both readings; the majority take them as angels

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that the one who recites the Qur'an and has it by heart is with the noble and obedient scribes, using the two words that end this verse and open the next.
notes.src: agreed upon, from Aisha, reported by Bukhari and Muslim in their chapters on the merits of the Qur'an

notes.t: Hands are mentioned, which is a concrete thing to say about beings otherwise left undescribed. The chain the surah draws is physical: pages, hands, a reciter, a hearer.

links.why: honourable recorders who write and know what you do
who taught by the pen

16.sense: The scribes get two words of description and both are about character rather than power. They are noble, and they are obedient in the way a good child is obedient to a parent.

notes.t: Barara is the plural of barr, from birr, the same root as the duty a child owes a mother and father. The word chosen for angelic obedience is a family word and not a military one.
From verse thirteen to here the surah has given five descriptions and not one concerns the content of the pages. It establishes the standing of the message before saying a word about its subject.
The Qur'an describes angels elsewhere as those who do not disobey what Allah commands them and who do what they are ordered.

links.why: honoured servants who do not speak ahead of Him
angels who do not disobey what they are commanded

17.sense: After five verses on the honour of the pages, the turn to the human being is abrupt. He is cursed, and then exclaimed over, and the thing exclaimed over is the size of his refusal.

notes.t: Qutila is literally may he be killed. Arabic used it as a curse the way English once used may he perish, and the exegetes read it as a statement of what such a man deserves rather than as a wish being made.
Ma akfarahu is the Arabic exclamatory form, the same construction as how good this is. Turned on kufr it asks what quantity of denial a creature would have to hold in order to behave like this.

The root k-f-r covers denial and ingratitude, and its first sense in the language is to cover a thing over. Which sense governs here is discussed, and the verses that follow, about a man's own manufacture, push towards ingratitude.
notes.src: the exegetes divide between kufr as denial and kufr as ingratitude in this verse

links.why: man is indeed given to wrong and to ingratitude
man is ungrateful to his Lord, and he witnesses that himself

18.sense: A question about material. Out of what did He make him. It is put to a man who has just been called ungrateful, and the answer will be the shortest available correction of his estimate of himself.

notes.t: The question is not asking for information. It asks a person who is behaving as though he were self-made to name his own raw material out loud.
This verse and the five that follow are one continuous sentence broken across six verse endings, and every ending rhymes on the same suffix. The passage is built to be heard rather than read.
The Qur'an asks the same question elsewhere and answers it the same way, tracing a man back to a drop, then to clay, then to dust.

links.why: the stages of a man's making set out as an argument for resurrection
was there not a period when he was not a thing worth mentioning

19.sense: The answer. From a drop, and after that a measuring out. Creation is given in two motions: the material, which is negligible, and the determination, which is exact.

notes.t: Nutfa in Arabic is the small amount of water left in the bottom of a bucket or a waterskin, a residue. The word was chosen for its smallness, not for its biology.

Qaddara is from qadr, measure. It covers apportioning a thing's size, its capacities and its span. The measuring comes after the making, which is the order the surah keeps for everything else it lists.
The Qur'an sets out the stages after the drop in another place, naming a clot, a lump, bones and then flesh, and calls the result another creation.

links.why: the stages of forming, given in sequence
was he not a drop of fluid emitted, then a clot

20.sense: Then the way was made easy. The object is placed before the verb, which in Arabic narrows it: this particular way, and no other, was the one smoothed for him.

notes.t: The way is read in two directions. Some of the earliest exegetes take it as the exit from the womb, which fits a sequence that runs making, birth, death and burial. Others take it as the road of guidance, made passable for him.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both readings from the earliest generations

notes.t: Yassara is to make a thing easy, not to force anyone down it. On the second reading the verse says the road was cleared, not that a person was walked along it.
The Qur'an says elsewhere that man was shown the two ascents and left to attempt one of them, which keeps the same division between showing and walking.

links.why: We guided him to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful
and We showed him the two heights

21.sense: Death is listed as something done to him, and then a second act follows it. He was not merely left where he fell. He was given a grave, and the grave is counted among the things he received.

notes.t: Aqbara is not the ordinary verb for burying, which is qabara. The fourth form means to cause a thing to have a grave, or to grant one. The Arabic makes burial a provision rather than a disposal.
Concealing the dead is close to universal among human beings and close to absent among other animals. The verse counts the practice among the things done for man rather than by him.
The Qur'an shows the first burial being taught to a human being by a crow scratching the ground, after the first killing.

links.why: the crow that showed the son of Adam how to bury his brother
did We not make the earth a container for the living and the dead

22.sense: The last item in the sequence is the only one with a condition attached. The making, the measuring, the easing, the dying and the burying are all stated flatly. The raising is stated as when He wills, which puts the timing out of reach.

notes.t: Nashara is to spread a thing out, the verb for unrolling a cloth or opening a scroll. The fourth form used here is the Qur'an's word for raising the dead, and the image is of something folded away being opened out again.

The whole sequence from verse eighteen tracks one man in the singular, from a drop to a resurrection. The Qur'an argues resurrection this way repeatedly: whoever managed the first thing is not strained by the second.
The argument is made explicit elsewhere, that He begins the creation and then repeats it, and the repeating is easier for Him.

links.why: He begins creation and repeats it, and that is easier for Him
who will give life to bones after they have crumbled

23.sense: A second hard stop, and a verdict drawn from the sequence just given. All of that was done for him and he has still not done the thing he was told to do.

notes.t: Lamma is not the same particle as lam. Lam means did not; lamma means has not yet, and it leaves the door open for the thing still to be done. The grammar is harsher than lam in its accusation and gentler in what it expects.
What was commanded is not specified, which lets the verse land on any reader without having to name his particular omission first.
Kalla appears twice in this surah, at verse eleven and here, and on both occasions it turns the surah onto a new subject rather than closing an argument.

links.why: does man think he will be left to no purpose
did you think We created you in vain

24.sense: The instruction is to look at something already on the table. Not at the stars, not at a miracle, at lunch. The next eight verses take the plate apart backwards, from the food to the plants to the split ground to the rain.

notes.t: Fal-yanzur is an imperative of command, let him look. The Qur'an issues it about several ordinary things, and here the ordinary thing is the least remarkable object in the room.

Looking at food and following it back is a chain that ends in something no human being did. That is the argument of the whole passage, and the surah leaves the reader to walk it rather than stating it.
The identical command opens the same kind of argument in another short surah, where the thing to be looked at is what a man was made from.

links.why: the same command, turned on what he was created from
have you seen what you sow, do you plant it or are We the planter

25.sense: The chain starts at the top. Water was poured, and the verb is repeated in its noun form directly after itself, which is how Arabic says the action was done thoroughly.

notes.t: Sabba is to pour from above, the verb for tipping a vessel out. It is not the usual word for rain, which is anzala or amtara, and it makes the sky sound like something being emptied.
Sababna sabban is the absolute object, an Arabic device in which a verb's own verbal noun is added to intensify it. The device recurs in the next verse and gives this passage its rhythm.
The order of the passage runs water, then earth, then plants, then the animals that eat them, which is the order a farmer would give if asked where his bread began.

links.why: have you seen the water you drink, did you send it down from the clouds
water sent down in torrents to bring out grain and plants

26.sense: The ground is opened. The verse does not say the seed pushed through; it says We split, which assigns the small violence of germination to the same hand that poured the rain.

notes.t: Shaqq is a tearing or a cleaving. The Qur'an uses the same root for the sky splitting open on the Last Day, which puts a seed breaking soil and the end of the world inside one vocabulary.
A seed lifting a crust of dry earth is one of the few forces in nature slow enough and small enough to be missed entirely. The verse names it as a deliberate act.
The Qur'an says elsewhere that Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date stone, using a different verb for the same event.

links.why: the splitter of the grain and the date stone
the same root used of the sky splitting open

27.sense: The first thing named out of the split ground is grain, which is what most of the world eats on most days. The list that follows moves outward from the staple to the luxuries and ends with fodder.

notes.t: Habb is grain taken as a mass, wheat and barley, the crop that is stored and ground rather than picked and eaten on the spot. It is put first because it is the base of the diet.
The verb is causative, anbatna, We made grow, not nabata, it grew. Every verb in this passage keeps the agency on the same side of the sentence.
The Qur'an describes the same crop elsewhere as grain brought out in stacked layers from a green shoot, and treats it as a sign in its own right.

links.why: grain in stacked layers brought out of green shoots
the dead earth revived and grain brought out of it to eat

28.sense: Grapes next, and then qadb, a green crop cut fresh. One is a fruit eaten for pleasure and the other is cut and carried to animals, and the verse puts them in the same breath without ranking them.

notes.t: Qadb comes from the root for cutting. It names a plant harvested green and cut again as it regrows, what a farmer would call a cutting crop, usually understood as alfalfa or something close to it.
Grapes and dates are the two fruits the Qur'an names most often, and almost always in lists like this one about what comes out of the ground.
A nearly identical short list of crops appears in another surah, where it closes with the statement that in this is a sign for people who reflect.

links.why: the same short list of crops, ending in a call to reflect
a garden of palms and grapevines used as a parable

29.sense: Two trees, both of which take years to bear and then bear for generations. Unlike the grain and the fodder, these are crops a man plants for people he will not meet.

notes.t: Olive and date are the two trees an Arabian or Mediterranean household lived off: oil and lamplight from one, fruit and sugar from the other, timber and rope and shade from both.
The list has now moved from an annual crop to a perennial one, and from what a family eats this year to what it inherits and passes on.
The Qur'an swears by the olive at the head of another surah, and uses the olive tree in the parable of the light as one neither of the east nor of the west.

links.why: an oath by the fig and the olive
the palm trunk Maryam was told to shake

30.sense: Enclosed gardens, and the adjective given them is one Arabic uses of thick necks and heavy shoulders. The picture is of growth crowded together and too dense to see through.

notes.t: Hadiqa is specifically a walled or enclosed garden, distinct from an open field. The word carries a boundary inside it, and a boundary implies somebody who built it.

Ghulb is the plural of aghlab, used in Arabic of a man with a thick neck and by extension of trees with heavy trunks standing close. Applying a body word to an orchard is ordinary in Arabic and hard to carry into English.
The exegetes gloss ghulb as thick-trunked, as tall, and as tangled together. The glosses overlap rather than compete, and all of them describe an orchard that has been left to grow.
notes.src: at-Tabari collects the glosses of the early exegetes without ranking them

links.why: gardens trellised and untrellised, listed the same way
the same word for gardens, paired again with grapevines

31.sense: The list closes on a pair: fruit, which people eat, and abb, which the exegetes take as the grazing that animals eat. The next verse will say plainly which is meant for whom.

notes.t: Abb is one of the rarer words in the Qur'an. It is reported that Umar recited this verse and said that he knew what fakiha was but asked what abb is, and then checked himself for pressing the question. The report is well known and its wording varies between collections.
notes.src: transmitted from Umar in several wordings by al-Hakim and others; the chains are discussed

notes.t: Both readings of the word, dry pasture and fresh herbage, agree that it is what beasts eat rather than what people eat, which is what lets the next verse divide the whole list between you and your livestock.
Fakiha is fruit eaten for enjoyment rather than for sustenance, which is why the Qur'an uses the word so often for what grows in the Garden.

links.why: in it is fruit, and palms with sheathed clusters
the sentence that closes this same list in the surah before

32.sense: The eight verses of rain and crops are closed with a purpose clause. All of it was provisioning, and the provisioning includes the animals, which are named as yours, since a man's herd is part of what feeds him.

notes.t: Mataʿ is goods for use. The Qur'an uses it steadily for things that are real, useful and temporary, and the word has an expiry built into it.
This exact sentence, word for word, closes the same argument in the surah immediately before this one, which is one of several joins between the two.
The address switches to you and your for the first time since verse ten. The passage has been about man in the third person, and it lands on the reader at the moment the food arrives.

links.why: the identical sentence closing the identical argument
the livestock He created for you, warmth and benefits and food

33.sense: The turn is immediate. One verse ago there was fruit and pasture, and now there is a noise that ends it. The Day is named by its sound rather than by its date.

notes.t: Sakhkha in the language is a sound loud enough to deafen whoever hears it. The word occurs only here in the Qur'an, and it names the event by what it does to an ear.
The Qur'an gives the Last Day many names and most of them describe an effect rather than a time: the striking, the overwhelming, the calamity, the deafening. None of them is a date.
The trumpet blast is described in another surah as the thing at which everyone in the heavens and the earth falls down, except whom Allah wills.

links.why: the striking, and what will make you know what the striking is
the blast on the trumpet and what it does to everyone at once

34.sense: The list of people fled from begins with a brother. It will run through a whole household in the next two verses, and it starts with the one a man grew up beside.

notes.t: Firar is flight from danger. The verse does not say people are separated from each other; it says they run, which makes every one of them the one who is doing the leaving.
The list is built to be recognised. Whoever reads it has most of these people, and the surah names them one at a time rather than saying his family, so that nobody can generalise past it.
Another surah says that on that Day no close friend will ask after a close friend, though they will be put in sight of one another.

links.why: a man wishing to ransom himself with his sons, his wife and his brother
a day when no father avails his son and no son his father

35.sense: The parents, and the mother is placed before the father. The two people a man owes most to are the second pair he runs from.

notes.t: Mother before father is the order the Qur'an keeps when it speaks of what is owed to parents, and it is kept here too, inside a verse about abandonment.
These are the relations the Qur'an spends the most verses commanding care for. Naming them in this list measures the weight of the Day against the strongest obligations a person carries.
The Qur'an ties gratitude to parents and gratitude to Allah together in a single command, and mentions the mother's carrying and weaning by name.

links.why: be grateful to Me and to your parents, in one sentence
say not even a word of complaint to them

36.sense: The household is completed with the wife and the children, the people a man chose and the people he made. Six relations across three verses, and nobody is left out of the flight.

notes.t: Sahiba is literally the companion, the feminine of sahib. The Qur'an uses it for a wife in several places, naming her by the fact of company rather than by the contract.
The order across the three verses runs brother, mother, father, wife, children, moving from the family a man is born into to the family he builds. Both are left behind at the same speed.
Almost the same list, in almost the same order, appears in Surat al-Maʿarij as the ransom a criminal would offer for himself and cannot pay.

links.why: the same relations, offered as a ransom that is refused
no ties of kinship between them on that Day, and no asking after one another

words.g: that takes up all of him

37.sense: The reason for the flight is given, and it is not hatred. Each person has a matter of his own that uses up everything he has, and there is nothing left over to spend on anybody else.

notes.t: Yughnihi is from the same root as istaghna in verse five, the root of needing nothing. The man who once considered himself sufficient now has a concern that is sufficient to fill him. The surah puts the two uses at its two ends.
Shaʾn is a matter or an affair, the thing a person is currently occupied with. The verse does not say what it is, and the vagueness does the work: whatever it is, it is enough to use him up.
The Qur'an makes the same point with a specific image elsewhere, showing a nursing mother forgetting the child she is nursing when she sees the Hour.

links.why: every nursing mother forgetting what she nursed
a day when no soul holds any power for another soul

38.sense: After the noise and the running, the surah sorts everyone by their faces. The first group is lit up, and the word chosen for it is the word used of daybreak.

notes.t: Musfira is from the root s-f-r, the same root as asfara, used of the dawn breaking. A face described this way is one that has had a covering taken off it.

The lexicographers derive safara, the scribes of verse fifteen, and safar, travel, and sifr, a book, from that same sense of uncovering. On that reading the surah opens with pages held out and closes with faces uncovered.
Sorting people by their faces is one of the Qur'an's steadiest ways of describing that Day, and it uses the method in several surahs.

links.why: faces radiant and looking, and faces contorted
a day on which faces whiten and faces blacken

39.sense: The bright faces get two more words. They are laughing, which is something a body does without being instructed, and they are taking in good news.

notes.t: Laughter is rare in the Qur'an's descriptions of the Hereafter, and here it is placed without qualification. The word is the ordinary Arabic one for laughing out loud.
Mustabshira is the tenth form of bushra, good news. It is the face of somebody who has just been told something, and at this point in the surah the news itself has not been reported.
The Qur'an supplies the news elsewhere, in the words the angels bring down: do not fear and do not grieve, and receive the good tidings of the Garden.

links.why: the angels descending with the words of the good news
on that day those who believed will laugh

40.sense: The second group. Their faces have dust on them, which is something that settles from outside rather than a colour they are. The description is of a thing that has landed on them.

notes.t: Ghabara is the fine dust that hangs in the air after a road is travelled or a wall comes down. It is what a face looks like after a long walk with no water at the end of it.
The bright faces were described by what they were doing, laughing and receiving news. These are described by what is on them. The grammar keeps them on the receiving end throughout.
The Qur'an describes the faces of the wrongdoers elsewhere as though pieces of the night had been laid over them.

links.why: faces covered as though with pieces of a dark night
faces on that day humbled, labouring and worn out

41.sense: A second layer over the first. Under the dust there is a darkness rising, and the verb is one of being overtaken by something that cannot be shaken off.

notes.t: Rahiqa is to overtake a thing and press down on it. The Qur'an uses the same verb of humiliation covering a face, and it carries force rather than settling.
Qatara is the black of smoke, the soot that darkens whatever it touches. Dust and smoke together describe a face that has come through both a road and a fire.
These two verses give the exact opposite of verse thirty eight in the same number of strokes. One face has a covering taken off it; the other has two put on.

links.why: no blackness and no humiliation covers the faces of those who did good
the same verb, with humiliation as the thing that covers them

42.sense: Only at the end are the dusty faces named. Two words are given, one for what they refused to accept and one for how they lived, and the surah stops there without a further sentence.

notes.t: Kafara and fajara are two plurals on the same Arabic pattern, and they answer kiram and barara in verse sixteen, which are also two plurals on that pattern. The scribes were noble and dutiful; these are denying and dissolute. The surah closes its own frame.

Fujur is the breaking open of restraint, the opposite of birr. The root also gives fajr, the dawn, because the dawn breaks the night open. Applied to conduct it names a person who has burst his limits.
The Qur'an pairs the same two words in the singular in the prayer of Nuh, where he says his people would beget none but the wicked and the ungrateful.

links.why: the dutiful are in bliss and the wicked in a blaze, the same pair of words
the two words paired again in Nuh's prayer
